idiom_name: embedded base struct as first member + shared operations table
implementation_notes: C has no inheritance, so the layer supertype is a hand-written structure: a base struct holding the shared state, embedded as the first member of every layer type so that a pointer to the member can be cast to a pointer to the base, plus free functions taking the base pointer as their first argument for the behavior the layer shares. The first-member rule - the layout GObject formalises - makes the upcast a plain cast or &derived->base, and a shared table of function pointers supplies the polymorphic part when the layer needs it. GLib/GObject is the library route (G_DEFINE_TYPE, G_DECLARE_FINAL_TYPE, G_DECLARE_DERIVABLE_TYPE) and is worth adopting once reference counting, properties, signals or introspectable types are wanted; the hand-written form stays justified in kernels, firmware and embedded code that cannot link a type system.
pitfalls: Only one base can be recovered without offset arithmetic: a second embedded base needs container_of-style macros and per-type cast helpers, and the first-member shortcut silently stops being valid.

C has no constructors, so every factory must initialise the embedded base (id, version); an uninitialised base yields garbage in every shared function and is a classic source of layer-wide corruption.
A hand-rolled operations table tends to grow into a private object system duplicating what GObject already provides (refcounting, properties, signals, type-safe casts).
